units.text: Begin with dynamic routing on the left. BGP peers exchange prefixes and react to route changes. Verify both advertised and received routes on capable customer equipment; tunnel health alone does not prove route exchange.

Compare static routing in the center. Configure remote prefixes explicitly where supported and plan health detection and failover. Static configuration does not learn newly added networks automatically.

Follow the forward and return paths on the right, then the routing checklist below. Inspect subnet routes, gateway routing and the remote return route. Transit Gateway also needs the correct attachment association and propagation.

Return to the complete slide. Routes provide reachability, not authorization. Check security controls, overlapping addresses and symmetry where stateful devices require it. An encrypted tunnel can be healthy while the application remains unreachable.

Start with tunnel capacity on the left. Select the supported bandwidth option for the design. Large Bandwidth Tunnels require Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN; actual throughput still depends on traffic, packet size and customer equipment.

Move to equal-cost multipath in the center. Transit Gateway distributes flows across eligible VPN paths using dynamic routing. More aggregate capacity does not make one individual flow use every tunnel.

Inspect acceleration on the right. Global Accelerator brings supported internet VPN traffic onto the AWS network near the customer gateway. This improves the network path; it does not support Large Bandwidth Tunnels.

With the full slide visible, distinguish capacity, multiple paths and acceleration. Check feature compatibility, then test representative flows, latency, failover and the backup path. Investigate packet sizing when measured performance falls short.

Inspect the dedicated connection on the left. A physical Ethernet port serves the connection. Arrange delivery and the facility cross-connect, using the Letter of Authorization and Connecting Facility Assignment for that process.
Move to the hosted connection on the right. A Direct Connect Partner provisions capacity, which you accept in your AWS account. Confirm delivery, supported features and resilience with the partner.

Follow the lower sequence. Build the virtual interface with its VLAN and peer settings, establish BGP, then verify application access. A connected physical port does not prove that routes are being exchanged.

Return to the original full slide. Check AWS and customer route tables, security controls and the return path. Validate physical connectivity, the virtual interface, BGP and end-to-end application behavior as separate layers.

Start with the private virtual interface on the left. It reaches VPC resources using private addresses, through a virtual private gateway directly or a Direct Connect gateway with the appropriate associations.

Move to the public virtual interface in the center. It reaches AWS public service endpoints using public addresses and advertised AWS prefixes. It still uses Direct Connect transport and does not provide general internet transit.

Inspect the transit virtual interface on the right. It reaches Transit Gateways through a Direct Connect gateway. A private virtual interface cannot replace the transit interface required by this gateway design.

With all three options visible, choose by the destination and gateway model. Private addressing does not guarantee encryption. Verify gateway associations, BGP advertisements, return routes and any encryption requirements separately.
